ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Inspection | Midland, TX
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Midland, TX gas plants, tank batteries, compressor stations and pipe, on site. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Midland, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection for owners in Midland and across the Permian Basin: separators and heater treaters, tank batteries, gas processing and compression piping, produced-water systems and gathering lines. Technicians are mobilized to your site with calibrated flaw detectors, dual-element probes and step blocks, work to a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a UT inspection quote for your Midland site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Midland

Midland sits at the center of the Midland Basin, the eastern sub-basin of the Permian, and the steel in the surrounding counties is overwhelmingly oilfield process steel. Martin, Glasscock, Reagan, Upton and Midland counties carry cryogenic gas processing plants, high-pressure gathering pipe in 20-inch and 24-inch sizes, and compressor stations strung along those lines. Ahead of all of that sit the production facilities themselves: wellhead separators, heater treaters, free-water knockouts, atmospheric tanks and the produced-water handling that follows every barrel of oil.

Each of these has a corrosion story, and ultrasonic testing is how that story is read without shutting anything down. Typical Midland jobs include:

  • Wall thickness grids on separator and treater shells, heads and nozzle necks, where produced water and carbon dioxide thin the bottom of the vessel first.
  • Thickness readings at condition monitoring locations on process piping, elbows and tees downstream of compressors and in dehydration and amine service.
  • Tank shell and floor-edge thickness checks on storage and produced-water tanks.
  • Angle-beam examination of new and repaired groove welds on skid piping and pressure vessels built or modified in the shops that serve the basin.
  • Thickness checks on pipeline risers, launcher and receiver barrels and meter-run piping at gathering stations.

The common thread is that the owner needs a defensible number for remaining wall without taking equipment out of service, and that is what the method delivers.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends a sound pulse into the steel and times the echoes. For a thickness job the echo from the back wall gives the remaining wall directly; for a weld job, echoes from inside the weld show discontinuities that a visual check cannot reach. UT works on any dense, sound-conducting metal, so carbon steel, stainless and alloy piping all qualify, and it needs access to only one side.

Its limits matter as much as its strengths. A thickness gauge reports the wall under the probe, so a pit between two readings can be missed; this is why grids are laid out on a spacing the procedure states and why scanning with the A-scan visible is preferred over trusting a number alone. Heavy scale, loose coating and rough corrosion scatter the beam, so surface preparation comes first. Coarse-grained castings and some stainless welds attenuate sound and may need a different probe or a different method. Very thin wall, below what the probe can resolve, is measured with a different technique or flagged for another method. A UT report says what was reached and what was not, and we write it that way.

Codes and acceptance criteria behind Midland UT work

Oilfield pressure equipment is governed by a stack of documents. Thickness work on vessels and piping follows the owner's inspection program, usually built on API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground storage tanks. Responsibility for the inspection and the fitness decision rests with the owner's own authorized inspector; Atlantis performs the nondestructive examination and reports the data. Contact thickness measurement is generally performed to ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 5 and Article 23 (SE-797), and the numbers feed the owner's corrosion rate and remaining-life calculation.

Weld examination uses ASME Section V Article 4 for the technique, with acceptance coming from the construction code, for example ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessels or ASME B31.3 for process piping. Pipeline girth welds fall under API 1104 and the federal pipeline safety rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and in Texas intrastate pipeline safety is overseen by the Railroad Commission of Texas. Pressure vessels also sit under the state boiler law administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Process safety rules in OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 require mechanical integrity programs for covered facilities, and thickness data is the backbone of those programs. Our guide to ASME Section V Article 5 thickness measurement explains the technique requirements in plain terms.

How the ultrasonic work is done

For thickness, the technician calibrates the instrument on a step block of the same material, using a dual-element probe on corroded or pitted surfaces so the two crystals can separate the transmitted pulse from the echo. With the A-scan displayed, the technician watches the signal rather than trusting a number, which prevents the double-echo errors that can make thin wall read thick. Hot surfaces on heater treaters and compressor discharge piping call for high-temperature probes and couplant, and readings are corrected for temperature when the procedure requires it. Each reading is tied to a numbered location on a sketch so the same point can be measured again at the next interval, which is how corrosion rates become meaningful.

For welds, an angle-beam probe at 45, 60 or 70 degrees sends shear waves into the joint. A reference level is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, the weld and heat-affected zones are scanned from both sides where geometry allows, and indications are evaluated against the code's acceptance table. Lack of fusion, cracks and slag give distinct signal patterns, and a Level II interprets them with the procedure open on the tailgate.

Turning readings into corrosion rates and remaining life

A thickness survey is only the first half of the story. The value comes when two surveys of the same locations are compared. If a separator shell read one wall thickness at the last interval and a lower one today, the difference divided by the time between surveys is the corrosion rate, and the remaining wall above the required minimum divided by that rate is the remaining life. Owners in the Permian use those two figures to set the next inspection date, decide whether a vessel can stay in service, and plan replacements before they become emergencies. Short-term and long-term rates often differ when produced-water chemistry or flow changes, which is why consistent point numbering and retained raw data matter. We deliver readings in a format your inspection group or software can import, and we flag any location that reads below the minimum or shows a sudden change so your authorized inspector sees it first.

Who performs the work

Technicians who perform and interpret UT are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and calibrates equipment, performs the examination and evaluates results. An ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports; the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is an ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Procedures are written to the governing code and revision, and a procedure that does not match the code edition on your purchase order does not go to the field. If your own written practice needs work, our written practice development and Level III consulting pages describe the support.

What the UT report contains

A usable report lets the owner's inspector make decisions without a phone call. Ours identify the component and location, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and temperature, the technician and qualification level, and the date. For thickness jobs, a grid or sketch shows each reading with the nominal and minimum required wall beside it, and readings below the minimum are flagged. For weld jobs, each indication is recorded with location, length, amplitude and the accept or reject call against the named criteria. Raw readings are retained so a later survey can be compared point for point.

Planning a UT job in Midland

Several realities of the Permian shape a good plan. Summer surface temperatures on dark steel can exceed what standard probes and couplants tolerate, so high-temperature materials are specified in the scope, and winter nights can fall low enough to stiffen couplant and slow crews. Wind and blowing dust are routine, which affects surface preparation and protects the probe face from grit. Many sites are remote lease roads or gas plants with safety orientation, gate access and permit-to-work rules, so sending names and qualification records ahead of time avoids delays at the gate. Because Atlantis has no office in Midland, crews travel to your site, so we plan travel, lodging and the scope together, and turnaround and shutdown windows at plants and compressor stations are worth raising early so the job fits the outage. The Texas inspection services page covers the wider state picture.

UT, MT or PT for your Midland job

Choosing the method depends on the question. Use ultrasonic testing when the question is how much wall is left or whether a weld is sound through its thickness. Use magnetic particle inspection in Midland when the question is surface cracking on carbon or low-alloy steel, for example at weld toes on a skid or on lifting lugs. Use liquid penetrant testing in Midland for surface-breaking flaws on stainless and other non-magnetic alloys. Many owners combine them: thickness first to confirm the equipment is fit, then surface methods on the repairs. National pages on ultrasonic testing describe the method in general.

Training your own technicians in Midland

If you run your own program, qualifying employees is cheaper than traveling a contractor for routine work. Our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training are built around SNT-TC-1A, with practice in the UT simulator, and the Midland training page explains how courses and employer-run practicals fit together. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel; the training builds the knowledge and records.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing cost in Midland?
faq.a: Cost depends on the scope, the number of locations, surface preparation and travel to your site, so we quote each job individually. Send the equipment list and the access details through the quote link and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness on equipment that is in service?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Contact ultrasonic thickness readings are taken from the outside while the equipment runs, provided the surface is accessible, safe to approach and within the probe's temperature range. High-temperature surfaces need special probes and couplant.

faq.q: Do you have an office or lab in Midland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Midland. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and the scope, travel and access are planned with you before the job.

faq.q: How is UT different from magnetic particle or penetrant testing?
faq.a: Ultrasonic testing measures remaining wall and finds flaws inside a weld, while magnetic particle and penetrant testing find only flaws that reach the surface. The right method depends on whether your concern is thinning, internal weld quality or surface cracking.

faq.q: Which codes do your Midland UT reports reference?
faq.a: Reports reference the code on your purchase order, typically ASME Section V for technique, ASTM E797 for thickness, and the construction code's acceptance criteria such as ASME Section VIII, ASME B31.3 or API 1104. For in-service equipment, the owner's authorized inspector makes the fitness decision.

faq.q: Will you act as the API authorized inspector on our vessels?
faq.a: No. The API in-service codes keep your own authorized inspector as the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination, records the thickness data and delivers a report that your inspector uses for corrosion rates and remaining life.

faq.q: What surface preparation does UT need?
faq.a: The surface should be free of loose scale, flaking paint and heavy rust so the probe couples properly. Thin, well-bonded coatings can often be measured through, but the procedure states when this is acceptable, and rough corrosion may need wire brushing or grinding first.

faq.q: How accurate are ultrasonic thickness readings on pitted steel?
faq.a: Accuracy depends on calibration, probe choice and surface condition. Dual-element probes and an A-scan display help on pitted wall, but a probe reads only the metal beneath it, so the grid spacing in the procedure matters. The report states what the survey could and could not reach.

faq.q: Can you train our Midland technicians in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 training built around SNT-TC-1A, with simulator practice, and we can help you write the employer's written practice. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own personnel after the required training and experience.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Midland, TX | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing for Midland, TX oilfield skids, vessels, lifting gear and structural steel. Request an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Midland, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel for Midland and Permian Basin owners: weld toes on compressor and process skids, pressure vessel and separator welds, lifting lugs and rigging, and structural steel at oilfield service yards. Crews travel to your site carrying yokes, particles and light meters, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a mag particle testing quote for your Midland site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Midland

The Permian economy runs on moving steel. Compressors shake their frames, pumping units rock through every stroke, trucks and cranes lift heavy loads, and wind and temperature swings flex everything that stands outdoors. Fatigue cracks begin at the surface, usually at a weld toe or a sharp change of section, and that is exactly where a magnetic method looks first. In and around Midland the work typically includes:

  • Weld toes and attachment welds on compressor skids, pulsation bottle supports and pipe supports at gathering and processing stations.
  • Seam, nozzle and repair welds on separators, heater treaters and other carbon steel pressure vessels.
  • Lifting lugs, spreader bars, shackles, hooks and padeyes used by service companies and rig-up crews.
  • Structural steel on tank battery platforms, pipe racks and equipment frames.
  • Weld repair excavations, checked after grinding to confirm that the crack is gone before the welder starts.

These are inexpensive checks that prevent expensive failures, because a crack caught as a surface indication is a grinding job, not a replacement.

What magnetic particle testing finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection magnetizes the steel and applies fine iron particles. Where a crack or other discontinuity interrupts the magnetic field, a small leakage field forms and the particles gather there, outlining the flaw. The method is fast and very sensitive to tight surface cracks, and it finds slightly subsurface flaws too.

The restrictions are firm. It works only on ferromagnetic material, which means carbon and low-alloy steel; austenitic stainless steel and aluminum cannot be examined this way. It detects flaws at or near the surface, not deep inside a weld. Orientation matters, since a crack parallel to the field lines gives almost no signal, so each area is examined with the field in two directions roughly at right angles. Thick coatings, scale and oil reduce sensitivity and call for cleaning. Where the question is wall loss or internal weld quality, a different method is the right one, and we say so rather than stretching MT beyond its range.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Midland MT work

Technique requirements come from ASME Section V Article 7, and many owners also call out ASTM E709 as a guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Appendix 6 for MT methods and acceptance, process piping to ASME B31.3 uses its own examination clause and Table 341.3.2, and structural work falls under AWS D1.1. Pipeline welds fall under API 1104 and the federal pipeline safety rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with the Railroad Commission of Texas overseeing intrastate pipeline safety. Vessels and boilers also fall under the state boiler law administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. For covered facilities, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 requires mechanical integrity inspections following good engineering practice. Our explanation of ASME Section V Article 7 walks through the technique requirements in detail.

How the magnetic particle work is done

Most field work uses an electromagnetic yoke. The yoke's lifting power is verified before use: an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The technician places the yoke across the area, applies dry powder or a wet suspension, and watches the particles while the field is on. Each area is examined twice with the field turned about ninety degrees so cracks in any direction are caught. Prods are used where the code allows them and arcing risk is controlled.

Visible-light particles in contrasting colors are common for outdoor work on cleaned weld areas. Fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity but need UV-A light in a darkened area, which on a sunny Permian day usually means a tent or a shop. A field indicator confirms that the magnetic flux is adequate. After the examination, residual magnetism is checked and removed with demagnetization when it could affect welding, machining or later service. Indications are classified, measured and recorded, and relevant ones are compared with the acceptance table.

Preparing the surface and the work area

Magnetic particle work is only as good as the surface it is done on. Loose scale, heavy rust, oil, grease and thick paint all hold particles away from the steel or mask small indications, so the procedure states how clean the area must be and how far beyond the weld the cleaning extends. Wire brushing, light grinding or solvent wiping is normal on oilfield steel, and blast-cleaned weld areas give the cleanest results. Thin, tightly bonded coatings can sometimes be examined through if the procedure allows it, but the technician checks that sensitivity is still adequate. Sharp edges, threads and sudden changes of section need extra attention because they create nonrelevant indications that must be told apart from real ones. In dusty Permian conditions we also agree up front who provides access, scaffolding or lifts for overhead and elevated welds, because a poorly reached weld is a poorly examined weld.

Weld repairs, fatigue and what a technician looks for

Most surface cracks in oilfield equipment fall into a few families. Fatigue cracks grow from weld toes and sharp corners where repeated stress concentrates, and they often run across the weld at the toe of a support or lug. Hydrogen-assisted and cold cracks can appear in the heat-affected zone of thick or highly restrained welds shortly after welding. Service cracking can start at gouges, arc strikes and grinding marks left by earlier work. A technician reads the pattern of the indication to separate these from nonrelevant ones such as magnetic writing or the edge of a weld cap. When a crack is found, the usual path is to grind it out, re-examine the excavation to confirm it is gone, then weld and examine again. Doing that check carefully is the most economical protection an owner can buy against a repeat failure.

Who performs the work

Magnetic particle technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up equipment, performs the examination and interprets results; an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Procedure approval sits with Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Procedures follow the code edition on your contract, and if you need help aligning your own procedures, see our Level III consulting page.

Equipment checks that protect the result

A magnetic particle result is only credible if the equipment was proven before the examination. Yokes are checked for lifting power on the day they are used, light meters are verified against their calibration interval, and wet suspensions are tested for particle concentration with a settling tube so a weak bath does not hide indications. Particle batches are checked for contamination. For systems that rely on a pie gauge or a shim, the technician confirms the field strength and direction on the actual weld geometry rather than assuming it. If any check fails, the work stops until it is corrected, and the calibration records are listed on the report so the owner can confirm everything was in date. These steps take a few minutes and are the reason an indication, or the absence of one, can be relied on later in an audit or a failure investigation.

What the MT report contains

The report identifies the component and area examined, the procedure and revision, the technique and magnetizing method, the yoke or equipment serial numbers and last calibration, the particle type and color, the surface condition, the technician and qualification level, and the date. Each recordable indication is described with location, orientation and length, and the report states plainly whether it is accepted or rejected against the named criteria. Sketches or photographs mark where indications were found, so a welder or an owner's inspector can find the exact spot again. Areas that could not be examined, for instance because of access or coating, are listed so nobody assumes they were covered.

Planning an MT job in Midland

West Texas conditions affect magnetic particle work in practical ways. Summer surface temperatures on dark steel can dry wet particles too quickly and exceed the limits of some materials, so we plan early or late work and shade where the procedure requires it. Winter nights can be cold enough to slow wet suspensions. Wind blows dry powder away and dust fouls surfaces, which is why wet visible or screened work is often chosen. Sites range from city fabrication yards to remote gas plants and lease pads, many with safety orientation, gate access and permit-to-work rules, so sending technician names and qualification records ahead helps entry go smoothly. Because Atlantis has no office in Midland, crews travel to your site and the scope, travel and access are agreed before mobilization. The Texas inspection services page gives more context for statewide work.

MT, PT or UT for your Midland job

Use magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, where it is faster and more sensitive than penetrant. Use liquid penetrant testing in Midland when the material is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, or when the surface is not suited to magnetizing. Use ultrasonic testing in Midland when the question is remaining wall or weld quality below the surface. The national magnetic particle testing page and our MT versus PT comparison give more detail on choosing between methods.

Training your own technicians in Midland

Many Permian operators and service companies train their own people so routine surface checks do not wait on an outside crew. Our MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training are built around SNT-TC-1A, and the Midland training page explains how courses and employer practicals fit together. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel after training and experience requirements are met.

faq.q: What does magnetic particle inspection find?
faq.a: Magnetic particle inspection finds cracks, laps, seams and other discontinuities that are open to the surface or lie just beneath it in ferromagnetic steel. It does not find flaws deep inside a weld or measure remaining wall thickness.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be done on stainless steel?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless steel, because it is not ferromagnetic and cannot hold the magnetic field the method depends on. Liquid penetrant testing is the usual alternative for stainless and other non-magnetic alloys.

faq.q: Do you have an office or crew in Midland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Midland, so crews are mobilized to the site for the scope you agree, and the people on the job are qualified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A under our written practice. We plan travel and access with you first.

faq.q: Which standard do you use for MT in Midland?
faq.a: The technique follows ASME Section V Article 7 or the procedure your contract names, and acceptance comes from the construction code such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. The report cites the exact documents.

faq.q: Can you do mag particle work at night or in the cold?
faq.a: Often yes, if the procedure allows it. Cold slows wet suspensions and darkness actually helps fluorescent work, but each material has temperature limits in the procedure, so we confirm conditions and plan the scope with you before mobilizing.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required after MT?
faq.a: No. It is required when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service. The procedure states when it applies, and the technician checks the remaining field and records the result if demagnetization was needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent particles?
faq.a: Visible particles are colored and viewed in white light, which suits field work on cleaned welds. Fluorescent particles glow under UV-A light and detect finer indications, but they need a darkened area, so they are used where a tent or shop is available.

faq.q: Will you serve as the API authorized inspector for our equipment?
faq.a: No. The inspector of record stays your own authorized inspector under the API in-service codes. We carry out the magnetic particle examination and hand over the findings in a report your inspector can rely on for fitness decisions.

faq.q: Can you train our people in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training built around SNT-TC-1A and can help you write the employer's written practice. Your company certifies its own personnel once the required training and experience are documented.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Midland, TX | LPT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for Midland, TX stainless piping, alloy welds, valves and process equipment, Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Midland, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for Midland and Permian Basin owners: stainless and alloy piping welds at gas plants, valve bodies and wellhead components, aluminum and nickel alloy parts, and repair areas on equipment that cannot be magnetized. Crews travel to your site carrying penetrant systems, cleaners and developers, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a dye penetrant quote for your Midland site and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Midland

Penetrant testing earns its place wherever steel is not magnetic or the surface is too awkward to magnetize. The Midland Basin has plenty of that. Gas processing plants and compressor stations use stainless steel and corrosion-resistant alloys in amine, dehydration and sour-service piping. Wellheads, valves and instrument fittings include alloy bodies and sealing surfaces. Oilfield service shops weld and repair a wide range of parts, and a penetrant check is the quick, portable way to confirm a repair or a new weld is free of cracks that break the surface.

Typical PT work around Midland includes:

  • Root and cap passes on stainless steel and alloy piping welds in process and sour-service systems.
  • Weld overlay and repair areas on valve bodies, wellhead components and pressure-containing parts.
  • Aluminum and nickel alloy heat exchanger components and fabricated fittings.
  • Machined surfaces, threads and seal faces on rotating and reciprocating equipment.
  • Carbon steel welds where magnetizing is impractical because of geometry or surface condition.

Because the method needs no power and little equipment, it travels well to remote lease sites and plants.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

A penetrant is applied to a clean, dry surface and allowed to enter any discontinuity open to the surface. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped penetrant back out, forming a visible mark. Cracks, laps, porosity and lack of fusion at the surface show up clearly, and the method works on almost any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

The limit is that PT detects only surface-breaking discontinuities. A flaw sealed beneath the surface will not be found, and neither will thinning from corrosion. Anything that blocks the opening defeats the test: paint, oil, scale, smeared metal from grinding or blasting, and the residue of earlier chemical cleaning. Porous surfaces trap penetrant and create false indications. For these reasons surface preparation and pre-cleaning are part of the procedure rather than an afterthought, and the report notes the preparation used so the result can be trusted.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Midland PT work

Technique requirements come from ASME Section V Article 6, and many contracts also reference ASTM E165 for general industry practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural welds. Pipeline welds fall under API 1104 and the federal rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with the Railroad Commission of Texas overseeing intrastate pipeline safety. Pressure equipment also falls under the state boiler law administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 requires covered process facilities to run mechanical integrity programs that rely on this kind of inspection. Our guide to ASME Section V Article 6 explains the technique rules in plain language.

How the penetrant work is done

The sequence is pre-clean, apply, dwell, remove, develop, inspect and post-clean. First the surface is cleaned of oil, scale, paint and weld spatter and allowed to dry. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or dip and left to dwell for the time the procedure sets, which depends on the material, the type of flaw expected and the temperature. Excess is then removed, by solvent wipe for solvent-removable systems or by water rinse for water-washable ones, taking care not to wash penetrant out of real flaws. A thin, even coat of developer is applied and given time to bleed out indications.

Visible red dye systems suit most field work in white light, while fluorescent systems detect finer flaws but need a darkened area and UV-A light. Indications are evaluated within the developing time window, measured and recorded, and the part is cleaned afterward so residual chemicals do not affect welding, service or later coatings. For stainless and nickel alloys, penetrant materials are selected with low sulfur and halogen content so they do not harm the metal.

Reading indications: relevant, false and nonrelevant

Not every mark on a developed surface is a flaw, and part of a technician's skill is telling them apart. A relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity and is evaluated against the acceptance criteria. A nonrelevant indication comes from a feature of the part, such as a thread root, a sharp corner, a press fit or a rough weld ripple that holds penetrant. A false indication comes from the process itself, for instance penetrant left on the surface from poor removal, a fingerprint or a spill. The procedure tells the technician how to evaluate doubtful marks, usually by wiping the area, reapplying developer and watching the indication reform. Linear marks that bleed out quickly are typical of cracks, while rounded marks suggest porosity. Everything evaluated is recorded, including indications judged nonrelevant, so the owner can see the reasoning rather than only the verdict.

Pre-cleaning, post-cleaning and materials control

Cleaning is half the job in penetrant testing. Before the penetrant goes on, solvents, mechanical cleaning or both remove oil, paint and scale, and the surface is given time to dry so solvent does not dilute the penetrant or fill a crack. Grinding and blasting can smear metal over fine cracks, so the procedure may call for etching or other treatment on certain surfaces. After the examination, penetrant residue is removed so it does not interfere with welding, coating or service; on stainless and nickel alloys, post-cleaning also removes chemicals that could cause trouble later. Penetrant materials are bought as a matched family, tracked by batch number and checked for contaminant content when the alloy requires it, and a field check against a known cracked reference block confirms the system is still working. Skipping any of these steps can turn a test into a formality, and the report shows that each was done.

Who performs the work

Penetrant technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the examination and interprets results, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, approves the method and procedure. Procedures follow the code edition in your contract. If your own penetrant procedure needs review, the Level III consulting page describes how we can help.

Choosing the penetrant system for the job

Penetrant systems differ in how they are removed and how sensitive they are, and the choice is made before the crew leaves for the site. Solvent-removable visible systems are the usual choice for field work on welds because they need no water and can be wiped off with cleaner. Water-washable systems suit rougher surfaces and larger areas, where wiping would be slow, but need care to avoid over-washing. Post-emulsifiable systems are used for the most critical parts and are rare in the field. Sensitivity levels range from low to very high; very fine cracks in alloy parts may justify a fluorescent system and a tent, while a rough weld in carbon steel will tolerate a visible dye. We match the system to the alloy, surface finish, expected flaw size, temperature and what the code allows, and we record the choice on the report so the method can be repeated at the next inspection.

What the PT report contains

Reports name the component and area, the procedure and revision, the penetrant family and method, the manufacturer and batch numbers of the penetrant, remover and developer, the surface preparation, the part and ambient temperatures, the dwell and development times, the technician and qualification level and the date. Each indication is described with location, size and type, with an accept or reject call against the named criteria and a sketch or photograph. Where an area could not be examined, for example because of insulation or access, the report lists it. Batch numbers matter because materials for stainless and nickel alloys must be traceable and verified for contaminant content.

Planning a PT job in Midland

Temperature governs penetrant work more than any other method. The standard range for the part and materials in ASME Section V Article 6 is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside it the procedure must be qualified for the actual temperature. Permian summers can push dark steel well past the upper limit and winter mornings fall below the lower one, so we plan for early or late work, shade or warming. Wind carries dust that settles on wet surfaces and sticks to developer, so sheltering the work area helps. Sites range from city fabrication shops to remote plants and lease roads with gate access, safety orientation and permit rules, so sending technician names and qualification records ahead avoids delays. Atlantis has no office in Midland, so crews travel to your site and the scope, travel and access are planned together. See the Texas inspection services page for statewide context.

PT, MT or UT for your Midland job

Choose liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws in stainless, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic materials, and for geometries that are awkward to magnetize. Choose magnetic particle inspection in Midland on carbon and low-alloy steel where speed and sensitivity matter. Choose ultrasonic testing in Midland when the concern is remaining wall or weld quality below the surface. The national penetrant testing page describes the method generally.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: Liquid penetrant testing finds cracks, laps, porosity and lack of fusion that are open to the surface of a non-porous material. It will not find flaws sealed beneath the surface or measure wall loss from corrosion.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be used on stainless steel and aluminum?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant testing works on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic metals that magnetic particle inspection cannot examine. Materials with low sulfur and halogen content are specified for stainless and nickel alloys.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 is about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside it, the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters in West Texas summers and winter mornings.

faq.q: Why is surface preparation so important for PT?
faq.a: Penetrant can only enter a flaw that is open and clean. Paint, scale, oil and smeared metal from grinding can seal a crack and hide it, so pre-cleaning is part of the procedure and the report records how the surface was prepared.

faq.q: How long does penetrant need to dwell on the surface?
faq.a: Dwell time is set by the procedure and depends on the material, the penetrant system, the expected flaw type and the temperature. The technician follows the stated time and records it, because too little dwell can miss tight cracks.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye penetrant is viewed in white light and suits most field work. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light, detects finer indications and requires a darkened area, so it is used where a tent or shop can be arranged.

faq.q: Will you act as the API authorized inspector on our equipment?
